job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Liam Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for a land surveying and roadworks firm in a small town near Linz. I studied civil engineering, and my final project was a plan for a footbridge over a stream in my home village. My days are half in the office checking measurements and half out in a high-vis jacket with the crew, and on Sundays I'm at church, where I help set up the hall.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like and what's hard in your day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the outdoors part and the feeling of finishing something you can walk on. What I find hard is the loan and living in a rented room above a bakery. I've about five days of money saved, and my family has nothing to spare, so I do everything on my own account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's look at AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, and that people have always worried about new machines. My grandfather said computers would end all the jobs, and they didn't. I'd tell friends that a bridge still needs someone to stand on it and say whether it's safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm anxious, but about my own money. I took the only job that was offered, the pay is low, and a firm like ours depends on a few road contracts. If the council cut those, we'd lose half the work in a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I do. I'd keep my head down, learn from the crew boss, take extra Saturday work when offered, and not use any AI tools. I'd put 50 a month aside and skip the trip home every second weekend, which saves the train fare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled on the surface. Underneath, I keep a quiet count of how much I owe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the firm depends on a few contracts. Who would you talk to about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The crew boss, Herr Gruber, who's been here thirty years. He'd say don't ask, just work, and he'd be right, because asking in this town makes people think you want out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why skip the trip home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's 28 euros each way, and it adds up. I'd call my mother on Sundays instead, and she'd say I should eat properly, and I'd say I do.

say: People always worry about new machines, and **a bridge** still needs someone to stand on it.
I'd tell friends computers didn't end the jobs either.
think: I'm anxious about **my own money**, since the firm depends on a few road contracts.
If the council cut them, we'd lose **half the work**.
do: Learn from the **crew boss** and take extra Saturday work.
Put **50 a month** aside and skip the trip home every second weekend.
feel: **Settled** on the surface, and quietly counting what I owe underneath.

fieldNote: His worry is the firm's few **road contracts** and his own debt.
Believes in staying quiet and working hard, a traditional habit that stops him asking.
Skips visits home to save money, a real sacrifice.

steps.text: Take extra Saturday work on the crew when offered
Move 50 a month into a savings account
Skip the train home every second weekend

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's look at Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a lot of talk, and that firms like ours will keep needing hands and eyes. I'd tell friends in offices to be careful, though. Some of it is real, and I'd be a fool to say it isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm worried. Checking measurements and drafting plans is thinking work, and a program that does it in minutes makes my desk half useless. The part I do outdoors stays, but the firm might ask for one engineer and a bigger crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move my hours to the field as much as I could and learn how to run a site. I'd ask Herr Gruber to teach me how to read the ground, not just the drawings. I wouldn't touch the AI tools, but I'd learn what they do from the office staff, so I can tell when a plan is wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, like a man who hears a rumour at church and can't tell if it's true. I keep wanting someone to tell me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't use the tools. Is that a rule?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a habit more than a rule. I trust what I've checked with my own tape, and I don't like putting my name under a number I didn't measure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your family say about you changing path?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My father would say do the honest work in front of you. He doesn't trust big changes, and I'm his son, so I don't either.

Firms like ours will keep needing hands and eyes.
think: Checking and drafting is **thinking work**, so my desk half could be useless.

fieldNote: He sees **hands-on work** as his protection and moves toward it.

steps.text: Spend most weeks on site learning to run a crew
Ask Herr Gruber to teach me to read the ground
Watch how the office staff cope before deciding anything

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's look at AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is too fast for anyone to cope with. Families and churches and towns need time to adjust, and I'd say that the people building it should answer for it. I'd tell friends to stick together and keep their savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm frightened. The office part of my job goes within the two years, and the crew part follows in 2031. I'd have a loan, a rented room and a skill that nobody needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything and go home to my parents' village for a while if the firm let me go. I'd work on a farm or in a workshop for food and a bed, because that is honest work and they'd take me. I'd also ask the pastor if the parish has a fund for people out of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd pray, and I'd also not sleep, which doesn't seem fair on the praying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd go home. What would your father say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say I told you so, but not unkindly. Then he'd put me to work in the barn the next morning, and that would be a relief.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The people who build it and sell it without asking us. I don't mean the machine. I mean the rich men who decided how fast it goes.

say: Two years is **too fast**, and the builders should answer for it.
Families, churches and towns need time to adjust.
think: The office part goes in two years and the **crew part** follows in 2031.
I'd have a loan and a **skill nobody needs**.
do: Cut all spending and go **home** to my parents' village if let go.
Work on a farm or workshop for **food and a bed**.
Ask the pastor about a **parish fund** for people out of work.
S2.quote: I don't mean the machine. I mean the rich men who decided how fast it goes.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose the job** and falls back on family and parish, not the state.
Blames wealthy decision-makers, not the technology.
Humour about prayer hides how scared he is.

steps.text: Cut all spending except rent and food
Move back to my parents' village if the firm lets me go
Ask the pastor about the parish fund for jobless members
Work for food and a bed on a neighbour's farm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's look at AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is a stretch but not nothing. I'd say that's enough time to look after your own, and I'd tell friends to save and keep their families close. I'd also say to learn a trade you can do with your hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd want out of the drawing office early, maybe in two years, and into site management or a bridge inspection role. I'd feel steadier with the 2034 date for robots, because that gives hands-on work more time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pay down my loan as fast as I could, and take the site manager course at the technical college in the evenings. I'd ask the firm to put me on bridge inspection work. I'd also help the parish with its building repairs on weekends, which counts as practice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less frightened. A plan to build on is like a footing for a wall, and I can feel it settle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why bridge inspection?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a person has to go there, climb under it and tell the council whether it's safe. People trust a face and a signature, and I don't think that changes quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I saw robots doing inspections in other towns before 2031. Then I'd stop betting on my hands and look at what else I could do.

say: Five years is a stretch, so **look after your own** and learn a trade.
I'd tell friends to save and keep family close.
think: I'd want out of the **drawing office** early and into site management.
The 2034 robot date gives **hands-on work** more time.
do: Pay down the **loan** as fast as I can.
Take the **site manager** course at the technical college in the evenings.
Ask the firm for **bridge inspection** work.
feel: **Less frightened**, since a plan is like a footing for a wall.
S3.quote: People trust a face and a signature, and I don't think that changes quickly.
fieldNote: Time lets him build a plan around **hands-on trust**.

steps.text: Take the site manager course at the technical college
Ask for bridge inspection work in the next year
Pay 120 a month toward the student loan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's look at AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is long enough for most people to find their feet, and I'd say so. I'd say the answer is work, family and community, not waiting for someone to hand us a solution.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel quite settled. At 32 I'd hope to be married, running sites and out of debt. Honestly, ten years is also long enough for the whole thing to look different from the card, and I'd keep that in mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work, clear the loan within six years, and finish my site manager qualification. I'd save for a small house in my home village, where my family is, and be active in the parish. And I'd carry on with a tape measure and no AI, because the old methods have saved me from mistakes more than once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm enough. I'd still count my money each month, but it wouldn't weigh on me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd carry on without AI. Do you worry about being left behind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little, yes. If the whole industry used it, I'd have to. But I'd learn it from someone I trust, in my own time, and not because a salesman told me to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your own children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To learn a skill with their hands as well as their heads, and to marry someone who'd stay. A job can leave you, and a family stays.

say: Ten years is long enough, and the answer is **work, family and community**.
We shouldn't wait for someone to hand us a solution.
think: At 32 I'd hope to be **married**, running sites and out of debt.
Ten years may make things look **different** from the card.
do: Clear the **loan** in six years and finish the site manager qualification.
Save for a small **house** in my home village.
Stay active in the **parish** and keep using a tape measure.
feel: **Calm enough**, still counting my money each month.
S4.quote: A job can leave you, and a family stays.
fieldNote: Time moves him to **uneasy**, with family and faith as his anchor.
Willing to learn AI later if the industry demands it, from someone he trusts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'd have no money, a loan and a skill the world doesn't want, and nobody in my family could rescue me. What would help is a job that stays local and honest, and a government that doesn't pretend the loan isn't a burden.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that young men like me do worry, even if we don't say it. We were told to study hard and work hard, and now we're told the rules have changed.

headlineQuote: We were told to study hard and work hard, and now we're told the rules have changed.
portrait: Liam, 22, is a top civil engineering graduate in his first job at a **surveying and roadworks firm** near Linz.
He has heavy debt, about five days of savings and no family help, and rents a room above a bakery.
He is traditional and resistant, avoids AI tools and trusts what he has measured himself.
He turns to **hands-on site work**, family and the parish rather than to the state or new technology.
He is anxious in most worlds, alarmed in 2028, and only uneasy with ten years to plan.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** scenario worries him most, since he would have a loan and no skill the world wants.
whatWouldHelp: Honest **local jobs**, and a government that admits the loan is a burden.
